title: The Secondary Sector: The Manufacturing Industry
summary: The meaning, features, importance and Nigerian problems of manufacturing.

p: Economic activity is grouped into the primary sector (farming, fishing, mining), the secondary sector (manufacturing and construction) and the tertiary sector (services). The secondary sector is the engine of industrialisation, turning raw materials into finished products.

img.alt: A factory turning raw materials into finished goods beside a crane building a structure from inputs, labelled manufacturing and construction

p: Manufacturing is the process of changing raw materials and intermediate goods into finished goods using machines, tools and labour. Examples: a textile mill turns cotton into fabric; a food factory turns tomatoes into tomato paste; a car plant assembles parts into a car; a soap or cement factory.

It is a secondary activity. It involves mass production in a factory. It is capital-intensive (it needs money for machines and technology). It makes tangible goods you can touch. It has strong linkages with other sectors: it buys from farms and mines and sells through traders and transporters.

1. Creates jobs for many skills (workers, engineers, managers). 2. Raises GDP. 3. Reduces import dependence and saves foreign exchange. 4. Creates linkages: a food factory gives farmers a market and transport firms business. 5. Earns foreign exchange when goods are exported. 6. Develops skills: it is a training ground for technical and managerial human capital.

1. Epileptic power supply: the number one problem. Factories run costly diesel generators, which raise costs and make products uncompetitive. 2. Poor infrastructure: bad roads, congested ports and weak railways raise transport costs. 3. Lack of finance: high interest rates and few long-term loans. 4. Foreign competition: cheap, often subsidised, imports flood the market, including dumping (selling abroad below cost). 5. Inconsistent government policy: sudden changes in tariffs, bans and taxes. 6. Shortage of skilled technicians and engineers.

As Minister of Industry: (1) Fix power by supporting embedded and renewable power for industrial clusters and special economic zones; (2) Provide long-term, low-interest finance through development banks; (3) Keep trade and tax policy stable for several years and train technicians through TVET, so that investors can plan.

title: The Construction Industry
summary: The meaning, features, importance and problems of the construction industry, and a comparison with manufacturing.

p: The construction industry is the part of the secondary sector concerned with planning, designing and building structures and infrastructure: roads, bridges, dams, railways, airports, houses, schools, hospitals and offices.

Project-based: every project is different. On-site work, not in a factory. Capital-intensive. A long gestation period (projects take long to finish). It is a good indicator of the health of the economy.

1. It builds the 'backbone' of infrastructure that every industry needs. 2. It employs many skilled (engineers, architects) and unskilled workers. 3. A boom in building signals that a country is investing and developing. 4. It stimulates demand for cement, steel, wood and glass, which helps manufacturing. 5. It provides schools, hospitals and homes, which improve the quality of life.

1. High and unstable cost of materials, especially cement. 2. Corruption: inflated contracts, kickbacks and poor-quality materials. 3. Abandoned projects: started and not finished because of a change of government, lack of funds or corruption. 4. Shortage of trained artisans (plumbers, electricians, masons, welders). 5. Funding problems: late payment for government jobs and high interest rates for private developers. 6. Collapsed buildings show the danger of weak regulation and poor materials.

(But a boom built on borrowed money and speculation can burst, as in some countries' house-price crashes.)

title: Financial Markets and Why They Must Be Regulated
summary: The money and capital markets, and the five reasons why the financial system needs referees.

p: Imagine a football match with no referee, no rules and no lines on the field: it would be chaos. The financial market is the 'field' where money and financial assets such as shares and bonds are traded. Without rules and referees, savings would be stolen, banks would collapse and the economy would fail.
A financial market is any marketplace where securities (financial assets) are traded. It connects lenders (people with spare money) to borrowers (people who need money).

head: Market
What
Time
Instruments
Purpose
rows: Treasury bills, commercial papers, bankers' acceptances
Long-term investment such as factories and government projects

p: 1. Protect investors and depositors from cheating and fraud. 2. Ensure financial stability: stop the collapse of a bank from causing a wider crisis (systemic risk). 3. Maintain confidence: people must feel safe to save and invest; if confidence is lost the system fails. 4. Prevent financial crime such as fraud, market manipulation and money laundering. 5. Ensure transparency: companies and banks must give clear, accurate and timely information.

Systemic risk is the danger that the failure of one bank or financial firm will spread to others and bring down the whole system, for example when depositors panic and rush to withdraw money (a bank run). Regulators prevent it by setting capital rules, supervising banks, insuring deposits and acting as a lender of last resort.

Depositors keep money in bank accounts and expect to get it back in full on demand; protection means deposit insurance and bank supervision. Investors buy shares or bonds and accept that prices may go up or down; protection means they must not be cheated, so they get true information, fair markets and punishment of fraud. The difference is that an investor's risk of a fall in market prices is not insured, but fraud and unfair practice are regulated.

title: The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
summary: The six functions of the CBN, its importance and its challenges.

p: The CBN is the apex regulator of the financial system, the 'banker's bank' and the government's bank.

1. Monetary policy management (its most important job): it controls money and credit to fight inflation and promote growth, using open market operations, the monetary policy rate (MPR) and the cash reserve ratio (CRR).
2. Banker and financial adviser to the government: it keeps the government's accounts, receives revenue, makes payments, and issues and manages government securities such as treasury bills.

3. Banker to other banks and lender of last resort: it holds commercial banks' accounts and lends to a bank that has a short-term shortage of cash so that a temporary problem does not become a collapse.
4. Issue of currency: it is the only body allowed to print and issue the naira.
5. Management of foreign reserves: it holds the country's reserves of dollars, pounds and other currencies to support the exchange rate and pay for imports.
6. Banking supervision: it licenses, supervises and examines banks to keep them safe and sound.

Importance: stable prices, a sound banking system and confidence in the naira. Challenges: balancing the fight against inflation (which needs high interest rates) with the need to promote growth (low rates); managing the exchange rate; and political interference.

Open market operations (buying or selling government securities to add or remove money); the MPR (the benchmark interest rate that shows the policy stance and affects all lending rates); the cash reserve ratio (the share of deposits that banks must keep with the CBN).
The monetary policy rate is set by the CBN's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which meets several times a year and announces whether to raise, cut or hold the rate.

title: The NDIC and the SEC
summary: Deposit insurance and bank failure resolution by the NDIC, investor protection and market regulation by the SEC, with the current insurance limit.

p: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation builds confidence in the banking system.

1. Deposit guarantee: it insures bank deposits up to a maximum. The lesson note gives ₦500,000, which was the old limit. In May 2024 the NDIC raised the maximum insured amount for deposit money banks to ₦5 million per depositor per bank (and also raised the limits for microfinance banks and others). If a bank fails, the NDIC pays insured depositors.
2. Banking supervision: it works with the CBN.
3. Failure resolution: when a bank cannot be saved, the NDIC is liquidator: it takes over, sells assets and pays depositors and other creditors.
Importance: it prevents bank runs. Challenges: recovering assets from directors of failed banks; moral hazard (banks may take more risks because depositors are insured).
The Securities and Exchange Commission is the apex regulator of the capital market.

1. Investor protection (its main duty) against fraud and unfair practice. 2. Regulation of the market: it registers and supervises operators such as the NGX, stockbrokers and issuing houses. 3. Registration of securities: any company selling shares or bonds to the public must register them with the SEC and publish a prospectus. 4. Market development: new products, investor education and openness. 5. Enforcement: it investigates insider trading and other abuses and can fine or ban operators.
Challenges: new products such as fintech and crypto-assets; low investor knowledge; enforcing rules against powerful persons.
Insider trading is buying or selling securities using secret, important information that is not yet public. It is unfair to other investors. The SEC is the agency responsible for fighting it.

sections.h: A failed bank: who does what?
p: The CBN licenses and supervises the bank and may revoke its licence. The NDIC then acts as liquidator and pays insured depositors. The SEC is involved only if the bank's shares are traded.

sections.h: Confidence is worth more than money
p: Is the NDIC more important for public confidence than for the money it pays out? Many economists say yes: because depositors know their savings are protected, they do not panic and queue to withdraw, so the existence of the insurance prevents the very crisis it covers.

title: The NGX, NAICOM and the Ministry of Finance
summary: How the exchange, the insurance regulator and the finance ministry fit into the system, and the difference between the SEC and the NGX.

p: Formerly the Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE). It is not a government regulator but a self-regulatory organisation: it is the marketplace itself, a company that provides the platform for trading shares and bonds.

Functions: 1. Provides a marketplace (now mostly electronic). 2. Sets listing requirements that a company must meet before its shares are traded (profit record, transparency, size). 3. Self-regulation: it makes and enforces conduct rules for its trading members, the stockbroking firms. 4. Price discovery: continuous buying and selling shows the market price of a share. 5. Provides market information on share prices and company performance.

The SEC regulates the whole capital market, including the NGX itself. The NGX regulates its own trading platform and its members. A company that wants its shares traded must meet the NGX listing requirements and have its offer registered with the SEC.

The National Insurance Commission is to insurance what the CBN is to banking. Functions: regulate and supervise all insurers and reinsurers; license new insurance companies, brokers and agents; protect policyholders (its main goal) by making sure that insurers can pay claims; ensure solvency by setting minimum capital (solvency margins); and approve new insurance products.
If insurance were unregulated, weak or dishonest firms could take premiums and refuse to pay claims, so people would stop trusting insurance and the risks of the economy would be higher.

It is the central policy-making arm of the federal government on financial matters. Roles: fiscal policy management (designing the tax and spending plan, the federal budget); managing public finance (revenue and spending); public debt management (domestic and external debts); policy oversight of agencies such as the CBN, SEC and NDIC; and formulating economic policy.

The Ministry of Finance deals with fiscal policy (taxes, spending, borrowing); the CBN deals with monetary policy (money supply and interest rates). Both aim at stable prices, growth and jobs, and they must work together.

title: International Trade: Meaning, Importance and Problems
summary: The meaning and types of international trade, the benefits and problems, and the infant industry argument.

p: Why does Nigeria not grow its own iPhones? Why does Japan buy crude oil from Nigeria? Because of international trade, the exchange of goods and services between countries. No country is self-sufficient. Trade lets countries specialise in what they do best, which raises efficiency and living standards.

Bilateral trade: between two countries (for example Nigeria and Ghana). Multilateral trade: among three or more countries, for example under the World Trade Organisation (WTO) or ECOWAS. Visible trade is in goods; invisible trade is in services.

1. Access to goods and services a country cannot produce, or cannot produce efficiently (Nigeria cannot grow apples). 2. A source of foreign exchange from exports to pay for imports. 3. Specialisation, which raises world output. 4. Larger markets and economies of scale (lower average cost from mass production). 5. Job creation in manufacturing, transport and farming for export. 6. Cooperation and cultural links.

1. Trade barriers: tariffs (taxes on imports) and quotas (limits on imports). 2. Exchange rate instability: a falling naira makes imports dear. 3. Dumping: selling at a price below cost in another country to destroy local industries. 4. Over-specialisation: dependence on one product (oil) exposes a country to price swings. 5. Infant industries cannot compete with large foreign firms without protection.

A new ('infant') industry has high costs because it is small and inexperienced. The argument is that the government should protect it temporarily with tariffs or quotas until it grows strong enough to compete. Danger: protection may last forever and leave the industry lazy and inefficient, and consumers pay higher prices.

Nigeria earns about 90% of its foreign exchange from crude oil. When oil prices fall, export earnings, government revenue and the naira all come under pressure. The remedy is diversification into agriculture, manufacturing and services.

title: Theories of Trade: Absolute and Comparative Advantage
summary: Adam Smith's absolute advantage and David Ricardo's comparative advantage, with worked examples and the solution to the rice and beans question.

p: A country has an absolute advantage in a good if it can produce more of it (or the same with fewer resources) than another country. Smith said each country should specialise in the goods in which it has an absolute advantage and trade.

Example: Ghana makes 20 units of cocoa and 2 laptops per worker; Japan makes 5 units of cocoa and 10 laptops. Ghana is better at cocoa (20 > 5) and Japan at laptops (10 > 2). Ghana should produce cocoa, Japan laptops, and they should trade.

What if one country is better at everything? A country has a comparative advantage in a good if it can produce it at a lower opportunity cost than the other. Opportunity cost is what you give up to produce something else. Ricardo showed that countries gain by specialising in the goods with the lowest opportunity cost, even without an absolute advantage.

Per day: Nigeria makes 6 wheat or 2 cloth; Chad makes 1 wheat or 1 cloth. Nigeria has an absolute advantage in both. Opportunity costs: Nigeria: 1 wheat = 2/6 = 0.33 cloth; 1 cloth = 6/2 = 3 wheat. Chad: 1 wheat = 1 cloth; 1 cloth = 1 wheat. Wheat: Nigeria's cost (0.33 cloth) is lower than Chad's (1 cloth), so Nigeria should specialise in wheat. Cloth: Chad's cost (1 wheat) is lower than Nigeria's (3 wheat), so Chad should specialise in cloth. Both can consume more than before by trading.

sections.h: The terms of trade must be between the two cost ratios
p: Both gain if 1 wheat trades for between 0.33 and 1 cloth. For example, at 1 wheat for 0.6 cloth, Nigeria gets 0.6 cloth for a wheat that costs it only 0.33 cloth, and Chad gets wheat for 0.6 cloth instead of 1 cloth.
Country A: 40 rice or 10 beans per acre. Country B: 20 rice or 5 beans.
(a) Absolute advantage: A in both rice (40 > 20) and beans (10 > 5).
(b) Opportunity cost of 1 rice: A = 10/40 = 0.25 beans; B = 5/20 = 0.25 beans.
(c) Opportunity cost of 1 bean: A = 40/10 = 4 rice; B = 20/5 = 4 rice.
(d) Comparative advantage: neither; the opportunity costs are the same.
(e) Trade: there are no gains from specialisation, because the opportunity costs are equal. (Trade could still help for other reasons, such as variety.)

title: Trade Barriers, Non-Tariff Barriers and the WTO
summary: Tariffs, quotas and non-tariff barriers, why governments use them, and the role of the World Trade Organisation.

p: A government may restrict imports to protect local producers, save foreign exchange or raise revenue. Tariffs are taxes on imports. Quotas are limits on the quantity that can be imported. Non-tariff barriers restrict trade in other ways.

1. Import licences and bans: only licensed firms may import, or certain goods are prohibited (for example, Nigeria's bans on some imports such as certain foods). 2. Quality and safety standards: strict rules on health, labelling or technical standards that foreign goods find costly to meet. 3. Administrative delays and customs procedures: slow clearance and heavy paperwork. Others: embargoes (a total ban on trade with a country), foreign exchange restrictions and subsidies to local producers.

To protect infant industries; to raise government revenue; to reduce a trade deficit; to discourage dumping; and to protect jobs. Disadvantages: consumers pay higher prices; inefficient industries survive; other countries may retaliate; and smuggling can increase.

The WTO is the international body, based in Geneva, that sets the rules of trade among its member countries, helps to reduce trade barriers through negotiation and settles trade disputes between members. It began in 1995 as the successor to the GATT agreement. Nigeria is a member.
Regional groups such as ECOWAS and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) aim to reduce barriers among members so that West African and African firms can sell in a larger market.

title: Economic Growth and Economic Development
summary: The meaning and difference of growth and development, real and nominal GDP, and why growth is necessary but not sufficient.

p: The words are often used together, but they mean different things. An economy can grow while many of its people remain poor.

img.alt: A picture of a plain pie labelled economic growth (pie size only) beside a pie being shared by a table of people labelled economic development, with improvements in living standards
img.cap: Growth is the size of the pie; development is how it is shared and used.

p: Economic growth is the increase in a country's total output of goods and services over time. It is a quantitative measure, usually the percentage rise in real GDP (GDP adjusted for inflation). Example: real GDP rises from ₦100 trillion to ₦103 trillion: growth = (103 – 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 3%.

Nominal GDP is measured at current prices, so it can rise just because prices rose. Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, so it shows the true change in output. That is why real GDP is the better measure of growth. Example: nominal GDP rises by 20% but prices rise 15%: real growth is only about 5%.

Economic development is a broader, qualitative idea: an improvement in the quality of life of the people. It includes growth plus better living standards, education, health and life expectancy, lower poverty and unemployment, political freedom and access to clean water and sanitation.
Study the table.

head: Feature
Economic growth
Economic development
rows: How the pie is shared and used

p: Growth without development is possible: in the 1970s oil boom Nigeria's GDP grew rapidly, but most people saw little improvement in schools, hospitals and roads. Development without growth is not possible: schools and doctors must be paid for from a growing economy. So growth is necessary but not sufficient for development.

If real GDP grows 5% and the population grows 5%, GDP per capita (GDP ÷ population) does not change, so the average person is no richer. For per capita income to rise, output must grow faster than population.

title: Indicators, Obstacles and Strategies for Development
summary: The measures of development (HDI and others), the obstacles in Nigeria and a three-point strategy.

p: Because GDP is not enough, economists also use: the Human Development Index (HDI) of the United Nations, which combines income (GNI per capita), health (life expectancy) and education (years of schooling); the infant mortality rate (babies who die before their first birthday, per 1,000 births); the literacy rate (share of adults who can read and write); and access to clean water and sanitation.

1. Corruption steals money meant for development. 2. Poor infrastructure, especially power, cripples industry. 3. Weak institutions and bad governance: inconsistent policies and weak rule of law. 4. Over-dependence on one commodity (oil). 5. Poor human capital: an uneducated, unhealthy workforce is unproductive.

1. Invest in human capital: fund and reform education and health. 2. Invest in infrastructure: reliable power, roads and ports. 3. Diversify the economy: agriculture, manufacturing and technology. 4. Fight corruption by openness and accountability in public spending. 5. Provide good governance: a stable, predictable and business-friendly climate.

(1) Fix electricity and transport so that factories and farms can work; (2) put more money into primary health care, basic education and technical training, with strict checks on spending; (3) open up trade and finance for small businesses and reduce corruption by publishing contracts and budgets.

Poverty and low income lead to poor health and malnutrition, then low productivity and lack of education, then unemployment, and back to poverty. Policies must break the cycle at several points at once.

title: The Balance of Payments: Structure and Accounts
summary: What the balance of payments records, the credit and debit rule, the current, capital and financial accounts, and surplus and deficit.

p: When Nigerians import cars from Japan, money flows out. When Nigeria exports crude oil, money flows in. When a Nigerian in the USA sends money home (remittances), money flows in. The balance of payments (BOP) is a country's official record of all economic transactions between its residents and the rest of the world over a period, usually a year. It is kept by double entry: credits (+) for transactions that bring money in, debits (–) for those that send money out.

It records trade in goods and services, income and transfers: 1. Balance of trade (visible balance): exports of goods (+) minus imports of goods (–). 2. Balance of services (invisible balance): services sold abroad (a tourist paying a Nigerian hotel, +) and bought (shipping on a foreign ship, –). 3. Net income: income of Nigerians from abroad (+), and profits paid to foreigners (for example profit sent home by a foreign-owned company, –). 4. Net current transfers: remittances and aid received (+), aid sent out (–).
Balance of trade = exports of goods – imports of goods. Current account balance = balance of trade + balance of services + net income + net transfers.
A small account for non-financial transfers such as debt forgiveness and the transfer of patents and copyrights.

Flows of money for investment: foreign direct investment (FDI: long-term, such as foreigners building a factory in Nigeria, +; Nigerians investing abroad, –); portfolio investment (buying 'paper' assets such as shares and bonds, often short-term); and other investment such as loans.

In accounting terms the three accounts together always sum to zero (apart from small errors and omissions) because every transaction has two sides. In everyday economics we say there is a BOP surplus when credits exceed debits on the main items (money flowing in is more than flowing out, so reserves build up) and a BOP deficit when debits exceed credits (money flowing out is more than flowing in, so foreign reserves fall).

The balance of trade counts only visible goods; the balance of payments counts goods, services, income, transfers, capital and financial flows. A country can have a trade surplus but a BOP deficit if, for example, it pays heavy debt service.

(a) A Nigerian imports a car: debit. (b) Nigeria exports crude oil to the USA: credit. (c) A Nigerian in London sends money home: credit (current transfer). (d) A Nigerian company pays a dividend to its parent in South Africa: debit (income paid abroad). (e) A German company builds a factory in Lagos: credit (FDI).

title: Causes and Correction of BOP Deficits
summary: Why Nigeria often has BOP problems, and the policies used to correct them: devaluation, tariffs, spending cuts, supply-side policy and exchange controls.

p: 1. High import dependence: a large appetite for foreign cars, phones and clothes. 2. A narrow export base: reliance on oil means export earnings collapse when its price falls. 3. Capital flight: large (often illegal) movement of money out of the country. 4. Heavy external debt service: a large part of foreign earnings goes to repay loans. 5. Low foreign investment where the country seems unsafe or unprofitable.
1. Expenditure-switching policies (make imports dearer): devaluation, which makes the naira cheaper so that imports cost more and exports are cheaper to foreigners; and tariffs and quotas.

2. Expenditure-dampening policies (cut total spending): contractionary fiscal policy (higher taxes, less spending) and contractionary monetary policy (higher interest rates). Drawback: these can cause recession and unemployment.
3. Supply-side policies, the best long-term solution: export promotion and diversification into agriculture, manufacturing and technology so that the country earns more foreign exchange.
4. Foreign exchange controls: the government rations foreign currency and decides who may import what.

sections.h: How devaluation is meant to work
p: Suppose the naira falls from ₦500 to ₦1,000 per dollar. A Nigerian export priced at $10 now brings ₦10,000 instead of ₦5,000, so it is more attractive to producers, and foreigners find it cheaper in dollar terms. Imports priced in dollars cost twice as many naira, so people buy fewer. Exports rise, imports fall, and the BOP improves. For this to work, demand for exports and imports must be responsive (the Marshall-Lerner condition) and the country must be able to supply more exports. Note: when a currency is allowed to float down, as the naira has been since 2023, the correct word is depreciation; devaluation means an official, deliberate cut under a fixed rate.

FDI is a long-term investment in a physical business (a factory) with control; it is stable and brings jobs and technology. Portfolio investment is the purchase of shares and bonds without control; it is short-term and can leave quickly (hot money).

Diversification and export promotion, because they raise the supply of foreign exchange instead of just rationing demand. Short-term measures such as controls and tariffs only hide the problem and can cause shortages and smuggling.

title: Second Term Revision: Industry, Regulation, Trade, Development and BOP
summary: A checklist, formulas and quick answers for the second term.

p: Manufacturing and construction: meaning, features, importance, problems. Financial regulation: why, the three kinds of agency, the CBN, NDIC, SEC, NGX, NAICOM and the Ministry of Finance. International trade: benefits, problems, absolute and comparative advantage, barriers, WTO. Growth and development: indicators, obstacles, strategies. Balance of payments: accounts, causes of deficit, corrections.

Opportunity cost of A in terms of B = quantity of B given up ÷ quantity of A gained. Growth rate = (new real GDP – old) ÷ old × 100. GDP per capita = GDP ÷ population. Balance of trade = exports – imports of goods. Current account balance = BOT + services + net income + net transfers.

Who pays insured depositors of a failed bank? The NDIC (limit ₦5 million for commercial banks since 2024). Who regulates insurers? NAICOM. NGX is an SRO. Rice and beans question: no comparative advantage because both opportunity costs are equal. Real GDP and population both up 5%: per capita unchanged. Classification: car import debit; oil export credit; remittance credit; dividend to South Africa debit; FDI credit.
Draw a regulators chart; redo the comparative advantage tables; classify five new BOP transactions; write a paragraph on each obstacle to development; do a past paper in exam time and mark it.
